claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations and phase heterogeneities.

A multi-fidelity framework integrating reduced-order physics models with machine learning trained on segmented microstructures can reliably predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will reduce computational cost by roughly one order of magnitude relative to conventional first-principles and CALPHAD approaches.
Reduced-order physical models can capture discrete phase-boundary effects and elastic–plastic transitions in this alloy.
Supervised machine learning should be trained on segmented microstructural data from the hierarchical heterostructure.
The method is intended for room-temperature tensile and fracture testing at typical strain rates.
Reliable application requires input microstructural data that accurately represent the alloy’s phase distributions and chemical fluctuations.
Hierarchical interfaces and chemically fluctuating phases mediate dislocation nucleation.
Hierarchical interfaces and chemically fluctuating phases mediate crack initiation.
Physical laws encoded in reduced-order models can represent elastic response and fracture mechanics at phase boundaries.
Machine learning can interpolate across complex microstructural variations while retaining sensitivity to the hierarchical microstructure.
Combining reduced-order physics and machine learning can bypass computationally intensive ab initio calculations.
Predictions of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness will have approximately 5–10% average error relative to experiment.
Traditional full-scale first-principles methods impose large computational demands.
Traditional first-principles, CALPHAD, and unsegmented machine-learning models do not fully capture hierarchical heterostructural effects on fracture properties.
The method may cease to be reliable when phase distributions or interfacial characteristics fall outside the training-data range.
Unexpected secondary-phase or precipitate formation can significantly alter mechanical response and invalidate reduced-order-model assumptions.
Accuracy and computational-efficiency gains depend on the quality and representativeness of the segmented microstructural training data.
